artworks.title: The Lycurgus Cup
artworks.description: British Museum dichroic cage cup — Lycurgus trapped in Ambrosia's vine as Dionysus' revenge closes, ruby by transmission, green by reflection.

artworks.title: Lycurgus and Ambrosia (mosaic from Herculaneum)
artworks.description: Herculaneum mosaic — Lycurgus raising his axe against Ambrosia as she becomes the vine that will bind him.

artworks.title: Lycurgus
artworks.description: Pujol's Neoclassical Thracian king — Homer's first persecutor of Dionysus staged as a moral drama of hubris.

artworks.title: King Lycurgus of Thrace (relief from the Roman theatre at Philippi)
artworks.description: Philippi theatre relief — the Edonian king in the scaenae frons of a city under Dionysus' patronage.

popCulture.title: Lycurgus of Thrace
popCulture.description: The Edonian king who drove Dionysus' nurses with an ox-goad — Homer's first persecutor of the god, blinded and short-lived after.

popCulture.title: Iliad
popCulture.description: Iliad 6 — Diomedes recalls Lycurgus' hubris against Dionysus — the epic's warning that even heroes should not chase the god into the sea.

popCulture.title: The Bacchae
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides' Theban climax keeps the Lycurgus pattern alive — the king who insults Dionysus and is torn apart for it.
